source_title: Nicolas Cage Owns a Mysterious Pyramid in a Cemetery with Close Ties to New Orleans’ Haunted Past - People.com
source_excerpt:
The actor was spotted visiting the gravesite with his wife, Riko Shibata, in the early days of their relationship, but he’s remained tight-lipped about the purchase
In 2010, Nicolas Cage purchased a nine-foot tomb that stands in St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 in New Orleans, one of the city’s oldest cemeteries with ties to its haunted history
The pyramid is reported to have cost him $20,000; however, the Hollywood star has been hesitant to discuss it in interviews over the years
Before marrying his wife, Riko Shibata, the couple was photographed visiting the cemetery plot together in 2019, which he did explain in a later interview
Nicolas Cage is creating his own piece of history in one of New Orleans’ most historic — and rumored to be haunted — cemeteries.
In 2010, the National Treasure actor, 62, purchased land within St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, where the city’s first mayor, Étienne de Boré, and Marie Laveau, the legendary figure known as the Queen of Voodoo, were laid to rest. On it, he built a 9-foot-tall white pyramid. According to a March 2022 profile by GQ , the gravesite is rumored to have cost $20,000.
While the pyramid’s alleged purpose is to serve as Cage’s final resting place, he has not explicitly confirmed as much. There’s no name on the structure, which stands out amongst the cemetery’s more standard burial sites. Instead it bears the Latin inscription “omnia ab uno,” which translates to “Everything from One.”
In the already-famous cemetery, Cage’s mysterious tomb has become notorious. According to Ripley’s Believe It or Not , it “puzzles everyone, even people who give tours of the grave.”
It has also attracted curious tourists, some of whom have left red lipstick kisses on the white structure.
The pyramid stands in St. Louis Cemetery No. 1, New Orleans’ oldest cemetery, near the graves of the city’s first mayor, Étienne de Boré, and Marie Laveau, the legendary figure known as the Queen of Voodoo.
Cage himself has had little to say about the tomb. In his 2022 profile with GQ , he opted out of discussing the gravesite, saying, “I’m not going to talk about that.” However, when pressed on the topic, he told the journalist, who had visited the site, “Well. You can talk about it.”
The profile noted that Cage’s cemetery purchase came shortly after his father, August Coppola, died in October 2009.
“I’m told that in some parts of Asia, like Korea, that if you make your plans in advance, that it actually means good luck and you have a healthy life. Also, it’s just a wise thing to do to take pressure off your family,” the actor said during the conversation. “Who wants to be dealing with all that when someone’s passed on?”
He has also spoken about his deep connection to New Orleans.
Elsewhere in the interview, he described the city as where he “began to understand more of the romantic world,” adding, “This is a city that can have that dark side. It’s very present. And the reality is, we both know I’m probably never really going to leave New Orleans.”
“I became a man in New Orleans, if you know what I mean,” he also told The New York Times in August 2019. “The city has a soft spot in my heart, though there are things that can go horribly wrong there.”
While the pyramid remains shrouded in mystery, it does seem to hold a special place in his heart.
In February 2020 he was photographed at the site with a woman who was later identified as his wife, Riko Shibata . They tied the knot one year after the outing.
Speaking with GQ in July 2021, he addressed the visit, saying, “When you enter a new love, you want to show where you went to school. ‘This is my old neighborhood, I grew up in that house.’ “
He added, “When I was in Japan, where I met Riko, I wanted to see the places that were meaningful to her, the shrines in Kyoto. New Orleans is like the other city I grew up in, so it was meaningful for me to show her New Orleans.”
The pyramid is not the only historic New Orleans property that Cage has owned.
In 2007, he purchased the infamous LaLaurie Mansion, a property in the French Quarter associated with Madame LaLaurie, a 19th-century socialite infamous for her cruel treatment of slaves on her property. He sold the home, which is largely believed to be haunted, after going into foreclosure on it two years later, per local outlet WGNO .
In a September 2014 interview with Vanity Fair , Cage explained his reasoning for the purchase.
“I once lived in the most haunted house in America. The LaLaurie Mansion in New Orleans used to belong to Madame LaLaurie, a well-known 19th century socialite and serial killer,” he said, adding that he figured ”it would be a good place in which to write the great American horror novel. I didn’t get too far with the novel.”
While unconfirmed, New Orleans Historical reported that LaLaurie is believed to have been laid to rest in the same cemetery as Cage’s pyramid.
His ownership of her home is also rumored by some to have sparked a curse upon the actor, leading him to purchase his cemetery plot as a form of protection. However, GQ reported that a tour guide at the cemetery shot the whispers down, dubbing that rumor and others “a load of malarkey.”
The pyramid is just one of several unconventional purchases Cage has made throughout his career.
According to previous reporting from PEOPLE, the actor once spent $150 million on 15 homes, two islands, a dinosaur skull, a Lamborghini, exotic pets and a rare vintage comic book. Along with the house, Cage previously owned Our Lady of Perpetual Help Chapel in New Orleans.
His purchases also included a 40-acre private island that had been listed for $3 million. In 2006, he reportedly bought four luxury yachts for a combined $20 million, including one named Sarita that featured a jacuzzi and gym and could accommodate 12 guests.
